li.help: Light iron is thin steel: the panels of appliances, bicycle frames, gates and sheet. It is the most common grade in a yard and pays the least.

drum.help: The drum of a washing machine is stainless steel. Stainless sorted on its own pays more than light iron; this yard does not sort it, so the drum goes with light iron.

mot.help: An electric motor has copper windings inside a steel body, with cast aluminium end caps. Whole, it sells as electric motors. The motor bench takes it apart into its metals.

cab.help: Insulated cable is paid on the copper it holds. Stripped, the copper sells as bare bright or No.2, and the plastic goes to a licensed waste carrier.

bb.help: Bare bright is clean, bare, unalloyed copper wire with no coating, solder or insulation. It is the best copper grade a yard sells. The ticket line compares it with today's price of light iron.

no2.help: No.2 copper is unalloyed copper that is not clean: coated, tinned, painted or with some solder. It pays less than bare bright.

brs.help: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. Taps, valves and fittings are brass solids. Its price follows copper, at a lower level.

alw.help: Alloy wheels are cast aluminium. They are paid as clean wheels only when the tyres and the balance weights are off.

alcast.help: The end caps of an electric motor are cast aluminium. Cast aluminium can be melted into alloy ingot.

ci.help: Cast iron is hard and brittle: a sledgehammer breaks it, it does not bend. Foundries buy it to melt again.

hms.help: HMS is heavy melting steel: thick old steel cut to a size a steel mill's furnace takes. 80:20 is the usual mix of grade 1 and grade 2.

hmsu.help: Heavy steel that is not yet cut to size pays less. Cut with the torch to furnace size, it pays as HMS 80:20.

cbody.help: Once a car is depolluted and the parts that pay more are off, its body goes to a shredder. The shredder tears it into fist-sized pieces of steel.

bri.help: In the crucible, brass solids melt. The dross is skimmed off and the clean metal is cast as ingots. A foundry pays more for an ingot than for scrap.

dross.help: Dross is the crust skimmed off molten metal. It still holds some metal, so it is sold, not thrown away.

ali.help: Cast aluminium from wheels and end caps melts in the crucible and is cast as aluminium alloy ingot.

conv.help: A catalytic converter holds small amounts of platinum, palladium and rhodium. It is sold whole and paid on assay, after a lab has measured its metals. This one comes from a depolluted car with a treatment record.

ss.help: Stainless 304 holds chromium and nickel. A magnet hardly holds it, so the analyser names it at the scale. Sorted on its own it pays far more than light iron.

bzs.help: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin; brass is copper and zinc. They look alike. The analyser tells them apart, and bronze pays more.

bzi.help: Bronze solids melt in the induction furnace. The dross is skimmed off and the clean metal is cast as bronze ingot, which a foundry pays more for.

pbb.help: A lead-acid battery is broken first: the case becomes plastic chips, the lead becomes paste and grids. The lead smelter melts the paste into lead ingot under its filter.

zorba.help: Zorba is the mixed non-ferrous metal the eddy current throws out of the shredder's stream: aluminium, copper, brass and zinc. The sensor sorter sorts it into pure grades.

lib.help: Light iron pressed into bales is dense and easy to load, so a steel mill pays more for bales than for loose light iron.

foundry.line: Buys cast iron for its furnaces

glossary.line: A metal mixed from two or more metals, such as brass.

store.title: Scrap to Ingot
store.subtitle: Scrapyard & Metal Tycoon
store.shortDescription: Strip copper, weigh scrap by grade and pour brass ingots in your own yard.
store.promotionalText: Take over Cinder Lane Yard, a small licensed yard full of old stock. Steer your worker with one thumb and take a washing machine apart, piece by piece.
store.description:
Take over Cinder Lane Yard, a small licensed scrapyard full of old stock, and steer your worker with one thumb. Stop beside a washing machine and it comes apart, piece by piece: light iron panels, a whole motor, a counterweight for the rubble skip.

Every load goes on the platform scale and into its bay by grade, at the day's posted price. The price board shows each grade's price today, the days before it and one plain word: low day, usual or high day. Hold any bay for a better day. The flatbed from Tollbridge Metals collects every bay you have not held and pays by transfer.

The yard came with an old hand stripper and a bundle of cable. Strip it and bare bright copper comes off the spool, worth many times the iron. Further on, a small crucible under its extraction hood melts brass taps into brass ingots.

Buy better tools and wheeled carriers: a sledgehammer and angle grinder for cast iron, and a cutting torch for steel beams, tanks certified empty and the depolluted end-of-life car that came in from Cottle Demolition with its paperwork. Buy a hook-lift truck and fetch loads from Hob's Farm Clearance and Cottle Demolition. Every load is labelled with what is in it and its price before you hook it, and the weighbridge prints gross, tare and net.

Hire a yard hand, a cutter and a driver. Each takes over one step of the work, so the yard keeps earning while you are away, for a few hours.

From the first minute the industry table ranks your yard against rival firms by tonnes supplied, under one aim: the largest full metal recycling and resource supplier. The rival firms are simulated.

Every firm, place and price in the game is invented. Prices keep the trade's true proportions. No real money goes into or comes out of anything in the game.
